newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ABB seen posting respectable nine months.
newsitem.headline: ABB seen posting respectable nine months.

text.p: Electrical engineering giant ABB Asea Brown Boveri should show continued respectable growth in the first nine months of 1996 but below the soaring levels of last year, analysts said.

ABB's nine-month results, due on Tuesday, were expected to confirm a slowdown to more sustainable growth levels that was seen in half-year results, when net profit rose 22 percent as against a 41 percent surge in the same 1995 period.
Eleven analysts in London, Zurich and Stockholm surveyed by Reuters forecast an average group net profit for the first nine months of 1996 of $804.7 million, up 23.6 percent from a year earlier.
Forecasts for nine-month profit ranged from a low of $767 million to a high of $832 million.
"We should see a slowdown of sorts compared to last year, but still at a respectable level," said Angela Dean at Morgan Stanley in London.

ABB sales are likely to reflect this slowdown as analysts expect nine-month sales to rise by five percent to $24.49 billion from 1995's $23.32 billion, which was down from the 16 percent boost seen in the same 1995 period.

ABB does not publish a break-down of figures for each of its four divisions, so analysts said key points of interest would be any comments on developments at two divisions, Power Generation and Industrial and Building Systems.

"We will be looking for any signs of slowdown in power generation, because there is price pressure out there and because of lower interest rates on customer advances," said Eric Steinhauser from Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).

Chris Heminway at Lehman Brothers said any qualitative statements on industrial and building systems -- ABB's largest business segment -- would be read closely for signs of impact from the West European economic slump.
"The overall rate of sales growth is going to be slowing down because of the cyclical downturn, especially in industrial and building systems," he said.
For 1996 analysts forecast an average net profit of $1,310 million, slightly down from 1995's inflated $1,315 million. Forecasts range from a low of $1,165 million to a high of $1,400 million.
In 1997 ABB's reported net profit is forecast to rebound to $1,508 million.
ABB's results this year will also be marked by the Adtranz joint venture with Daimler-Benz AG in rail transportation.
Last year ABB merged its profitable transportation business with Daimler's struggling business and ABB's 1996 results will only reflect its 50 percent stake in Adtranz.

This 50 percent stake is smaller than ABB's previous transportation business and ABB's 1996 figures will thus suffer when compared with 1995, when the transportation business accounted for full-year operating earnings of $207 million.
Another effect of the merger was Daimler's one-time payment of $250 million to ABB, which helped boost the 1995 net profit by a huge 73 percent to $1,315 million.
ABB's slowdown this year also reflects a sluggish European economy and continuing cut-throat conditions in worldwide power business .

"We will be looking to see how much ABB can make up for these factors with its continuing shift of production from Europe to lower-cost emerging countries in Asia and elsewhere," said Eric Benli of Bank Leu in Zurich.
